item.title: Forcing Immediate Output from Subprocesses in Python: PTY vs Buffering Solutions
item.description:
“Forcing Immediate Output from Subprocesses in Python: PTY vs Buffering Solutions”

When executing external programs from Python using modules like subprocess, captured output often appears delayed, especially when the external program (like a Ruby script using puts without a newline immediately) buffers its output until a newline or buffer flush occurs. This post examines several techniques to force immediate or line-buffered output when interacting with child processes, often involving pseudo-terminals (PTY) or explicit buffering control.

item.title: Python Subprocess: Silencing Command Output to Dev Null
item.description:
“Python Subprocess: Silencing Command Output to Dev Null”

Several methods exist to achieve this, varying slightly based on the Python version and the specific subprocess function used. Let’s explore the most common and robust approaches.

Silencing Output with subprocess.call

For Python versions 3.3 and later, the subprocess module provides a direct way to redirect output to DEVNULL.

import subprocess

# Example command
command_to_run = ['echo', 'foo']

# Redirect stdout and stderr to DEVNULL
return_code = subprocess.call(command_to_run,
    stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)

print(f"Command executed with return code: {return_code}")

For older Python versions, including Python 2.7, you need to explicitly open os.devnull in write mode.

item.title: Execute Shell Commands and Capture Output in Python
item.description:
How to Execute Shell Commands and Capture Output in Python

Python’s subprocess module offers a powerful and flexible way to interact with the operating system’s shell. This guide delves into various methods for executing shell commands and capturing their standard output (stdout) and standard error (stderr).

Using subprocess.check_output (Older Python Versions & Backwards Compatibility)

For a straightforward approach that works across many Python versions (including Python 2.7), subprocess.check_output is a reliable choice. It executes a command and returns its standard output. If the command returns a non-zero exit code (indicating an error), it raises a CalledProcessError.

item.title: Solved: How to Capture Live Output from a Subprocess Command in Python
item.description: I’m currently employing a Python script to drive a hydrodynamics code and have encountered a challenge during simulation runs. When executing the simulation command directly via the command line, I receive detailed output regarding iterations, timing, and various simulation metrics. However, when using subprocess.Popen in my script to initiate the command, I find myself in a bind: while I can capture the output for logging purposes, I lose sight of the real-time progress of the code.
